paragraphs.text: McMurtry et al. (1992) studied 46 members of a large 5-generation kindred with familial benign (hypocalciuric) hypercalcemia and found that 19 were affected. In the 15 hypercalcemic members examined biochemically, serum immunoreactive PTH was measured in 3 separate immunoassays. Levels became supranormal by about age 30 years and appeared to increase further thereafter. Serum alkaline phosphatase activity and creatinine were normal, but serum inorganic phosphate was lower than in unaffected members of the kindred. Three of 5 affected adults older than 40 years who were studied radiographically had changes suggestive of osteomalacia. In one of them, a 51-year-old woman, iliac crest biopsy confirmed defective skeletal mineralization. McMurtry et al. (1992) concluded that the disorder in this kindred may not be totally benign, because osteomalacia, perhaps due to mild hypophosphatemia, can develop during adulthood. They raised the possibility that they had observed an unusual variant of FBH.

paragraphs.text: Hannan et al. (2010) performed linkage studies with 24 polymorphic loci in the Oklahoma kindred and obtained a peak lod score of 6.92 at zero recombination with D19S606. Recombinants in 3 individuals refined the FBHH3 locus to a 4.1-Mb interval on 19q13 flanked by D19S112 and rs245111. This interval contained 135 protein-coding genes and 24 predicted genes. The syntenic region on mouse chromosome 7 contains 4 Casr-related sequences (Gprc2a-rs), but these have no human homologs. Comparative analysis showed that 2 conserved segments were inverted and that an 11.6-Mb region containing 35 murine genes, including the 4 Gprc2a-rs genes, is absent from the human genome. FBHH3 therefore cannot be attributed to these genes.
